slides.title: Bishnoi- the ecological stewards
bullets: Bishnoi- the ecological stewards Rules: Not to cut trees Be compassionate to all living beings
slides.deep_explanation: This slide examines the historic Bishnoi community of Rajasthan, renowned as India's first ecological stewards. Founded by Guru Jambheshwar in the 15th century with 29 rules (including strict prohibitions against cutting green trees and harming wild animals), the Bishnois sacrificed 363 lives in 1730 led by Amrita Devi to protect sacred Khejri (Prosopis cineraria) trees from the Maharaja of Jodhpur's axemen, establishing the historical antecedent for modern forest conservation.

slides.deep_explanation: This slide covers the landmark Chipko Movement initiated in the 1970s in the Garhwal Himalayas of Uttarakhand (Reni village). When the state forest department allotted ash trees to a commercial sports goods manufacturer while denying local agricultural access, rural women led by Gaura Devi and environmentalists Sunderlal Bahuguna and Chandi Prasad Bhatt physically clung to trees ('Chipko' = to hug/cling). The movement forced a 15-year commercial logging moratorium across Himalayan catchment forests.

slides.deep_explanation: This slide details the Appiko Movement, the southern counterpart to Chipko launched in September 1983 in Salkani forest, Uttara Kannada (Karnataka). Villagers embraced trees to halt clear-cutting in the Western Ghats biodiversity hotspot. Appiko articulated three operational objectives encapsulated as 'Ubbesu' (save/protect), 'Belessu' (grow/plant), and 'Balesu' (rational use), focusing on the 5 Fs of rural subsistence: Food, Fodder, Fuel, Fertilizer, and Fiber.

slides.title: The Kunthipuzha River
bullets: The Kunthipuzha River 1970: the Kerala State Electricity Board (KSEB) (submergence of 8.3 sq km of moist EG forest ) 1971 – 72: Steven Green -Rom Whitaker (BNHS)
slides.deep_explanation: This slide analyzes the Save Silent Valley Movement (1970s–1980s) in Palakkad, Kerala. The Kerala State Electricity Board (KSEB) proposed a 120 MW hydroelectric dam across the Kunthipuzha River that would submerge 8.3 sq km of pristine tropical evergreen rainforest. Led by the Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (KSSP) and poet-activist Sugathakumari, the struggle successfully mobilized public opinion and scientific surveys of the endangered Lion-tailed Macaque, culminating in the cancellation of the dam and declaration of Silent Valley National Park in 1984.

slides.title: The construction of an average 24-kg
bullets: The construction of an average 24-kg computer and 27-cm monitor requires at least 240 kg of fossil fuel, 22 kg of chemicals and 1,500 kgs of water – or
slides.deep_explanation: This slide highlights the severe ecological footprint of electronics manufacturing. Constructing a typical 24-kg desktop computer and CRT/LCD monitor requires an astonishing 240 kg of fossil fuels, 22 kg of toxic specialty chemicals, and 1,500 kg (1.5 tons) of clean water. Unlike conventional heavy machinery where the product mass exceeds the raw manufacturing inputs, semiconductors and IT hardware exhibit an inverted 10:1 material footprint ratio, proving that embodied manufacturing impacts far surpass the device's operational electricity consumption.

slides.deep_explanation: This slide contrasts Moore's Law (Gordon Moore's 1965 empirical observation that transistor density on integrated circuits doubles approximately every 18-24 months) with environmental sustainability. slides.title: Thick and Thin Client ?
bullets: Thick and Thin Client ? “Thin Clients are small, silent devices that communicate with a central server
slides.deep_explanation: This slide evaluates the architectural comparison between Traditional Thick Clients (individual desktop PCs with local CPUs, hard drives, and 250W power supplies) and Thin Clients (compact, solid-state terminal appliances that offload computation to centralized server clusters). Thin clients consume only 10-20% of the electrical energy, lack moving parts (longer lifespan of 6-8 years vs 3-4 years for PCs), cost £210 vs £400 per workstation, and drastically curtail physical e-waste generation.

slides.title: What is E-waste?
bullets: What is E-waste? Electronic Waste (e-Waste) - waste electronic/electrical goods which are not fit for their originally intended use. such as computers, cellular phones, stereos, refrigerators, air conditioners, other consumer durables, etc.
slides.deep_explanation: This slide defines Electronic Waste (e-Waste)—discarded electrical and electronic equipment that is obsolete, broken, or end-of-life. E-waste represents the fastest-growing solid waste stream globally (over 50 million metric tons annually). Crucially, e-waste contains hazardous toxins including lead (in solder and CRT glass), cadmium (in rechargeable batteries and contacts), mercury (in backlights and switches), and brominated flame retardants (BFRs in plastics), necessitating strict adherence to the Basel Convention on hazardous waste trade.
